# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Read in context: the most informative document so far, with a few problems

This report directly tests what the earlier documents argued about: whether the gain lasts, whether the meetings explanation holds up, and whether timesheets miss work. Its main corrections to the earlier claims are well supported:

- **Against the Varga comment:** A randomised comparison at 24 months, using record-based output and system-log hours, still finds a gain (+8.5%, CI 3.4 to 13.8). "Entirely an artifact" does not survive.
- **Against the meta-analysis:** All four long-follow-up studies it relied on were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms my earlier concern that its "no decay" claim rested on the studies most prone to inflation.
- **On the meetings explanation:** A registered test, filed before the 24-month data existed, supports it. Retrospective baseline calendar data now show treated and control offices started at similar meeting levels (7.4 v 7.2 hours). That resolves the baseline gap I raised about the nine-month analysis.

But a problem the report doesn't notice affects its estimate of decay, and the mediation results need more scrutiny than they get.

## The arithmetic

| Item | Check |
|---|---|
| Output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 → +9.8% ✓ |
| Output per hour, system logs | 0.966 / 0.89 → +8.5% ✓ |
| Halden continuers, hours ratio | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%) ✓ |
| Halden continuers, output per hour | 96.8 / 0.866 → +11.8% ✓ |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 ✓ |

## Problems

### 1. Contamination of the control group may explain part of the "decay"

In month 15, two of the seven control offices ran a meeting audit, and their output per hour then rose 4.1%. The report treats this as a side observation about whether gains are possible without cutting hours. But it also directly affects the main estimate.

If control offices improved, the gap between treated and control offices narrows even if treated offices didn't change. As a rough guide, two of seven offices each improving by 4.1% would raise the control average by about 1.2 points. That is close to half of the 2.7-point fall on the like-for-like measure (12.5% → 9.8%).

So the observed decline mixes two things: fading in treated offices and improvement in control offices. The report should:

- Show treated and control trends separately.
- Estimate the 24-month effect with and without the two audited offices.
- Consider whether the audit happened because the nine-month report, with its meetings finding, had been published. If so, that is spillover from the trial itself, and it may continue.

The true decay could be smaller than reported. It could also be larger, if the treated offices' own trend is examined directly.

### 2. The summary compares different measures

The summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months". But 12.5% is a timesheet figure and 8.5% is a system-log figure, so the comparison overstates the decline. The like-for-like change is 12.5% → 9.8%, a fall of about a fifth. Section 5 says "about a quarter", which matches neither exactly. The decline should be quoted consistently, on one measure.

### 3. The log-time measure needs defining before the mediation results can be interpreted

The log measure is described as active time on the case-management system, recording time "working on cases". That raises a question the report doesn't answer: does it include meetings?

- **If logs count only time spent on cases,** meetings aren't in the denominator. Cutting meetings would then raise *total* case-work time, not output per log-hour. For meetings to mediate a gain in output per log-hour, they would have to work through something like fewer interruptions and less fragmented time. That is plausible but a different mechanism, and it should be stated.
- **If logs count all logged-in time, meetings included,** then cutting meetings raises output per hour partly by arithmetic, by removing hours that produce no cases. That is the "removing low-value time" story, and it is a legitimate finding, but it is not a change in how productive case-work hours are.

The same question bears on the claim that logs are the "stricter" measure. Logs could miss off-system work such as phone calls, reading or discussion. The statement that logs "show slightly more work than timesheets" is made only from percentage changes; the hours levels should be reported.

### 4. The mediation estimates are probably more uncertain than shown

- **Few real units.** The "larger sample of office-months" is still 14 offices. Office-months within an office are not independent. With a total effect whose interval runs from 3.4% to 13.8%, a share-mediated interval as tight as 28–66% is surprising. The report should confirm that standard errors are clustered by office, preferably with a small-sample correction.
- **Overlapping data.** The registered test is confirmatory in timing, but it uses the same offices and overlapping months as the exploratory finding. It is a stronger test, not an independent replication.
- **Mediators weren't randomised.** Offices whose managers cut meetings most may differ in leadership quality in ways that also raise output. The limitations section acknowledges unmeasured confounding, but it deserves more weight, since 47% is the result the report emphasises most.

### 5. Cost and backlog are still missing for the arm that continues

The report gives a cost estimate for the counter arm (a 9% higher cost per contact to restore service) but none for case-processing, the arm the county is keeping. Treated staff work about 12% fewer actual hours than control staff, against a 20% cut in scheduled hours. Any overtime is paid on top of unchanged salaries. Output per employee is −3.4%, with an interval reaching −8.0%.

Over 24 months, even a small shortfall can build a backlog. The report should give:

- Backlog size
- Compliance with statutory deadlines
- Cost per case closed

The overturn rate (3.2% v 3.0%) now has time for appeals to resolve, which addresses my earlier concern about lag, but it still lacks a confidence interval.

### 6. The counter-arm cost figure needs explaining

The staffing figure checks out. With 12% more staff each working 17% fewer hours, total hours are about 93% of baseline. At +6.7% per hour, that restores output to roughly baseline.

But the labour cost per contact then rises by about 12–13%, not 9%. The 9% figure presumably includes non-staff costs. That should be stated, since cost is the number the county acted on.

### 7. The Halden follow-up has its own selection problems

- **Response bias.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations with records responded. Organisations that reverted or struggled may have been less likely to reply.
- **A stretched category.** The summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations". But a marketing agency citing client deadlines is not coverage-bound work in the meta-analysis's sense. Putting it in that category after the fact overstates how cleanly reversion tracks work type. The honest reading is that demands for responsiveness to clients can cause problems in discretionary work too.
- **Fair framing.** Calling the continuers an upper bound for self-selected survivors is the right description.
- **An open issue.** R. Okafor, a Halden author, co-signs this report. It doesn't address the Varga comment's finding that the working paper misdescribed when and why organisations withdrew. A follow-up co-written by a Halden author is a natural place to correct that record.

### 8. The Varga novelty argument is weakened but not refuted

Twenty-four months removes the "fades by month ten" prediction, which in any case came from a miscalculated extrapolation. But Varga's argument was also that staff *knew the change was being evaluated*. That is still true in an ongoing trial, so awareness of being observed cannot yet be separated from a lasting effect. The partial decline is consistent with some initial effect fading. Results after the trial ends would test the rest.

## What is now reasonably settled

- **Discretionary work:** In the best evidence available, a 20% cut in scheduled hours becomes an 11–12% cut in actual hours. Output per hour rises by about 8–10% at two years, down from about 12% at nine months; part of that decline may reflect control offices improving. Output per employee is about 3% lower, and a larger loss can't be ruled out.
- **Coverage-bound work:** Reduced hours reduce output and service unless staff are added. The county ended the arm. Restoring service needed about 12% more staff.
- **Mechanism:** About half of the per-hour gain plausibly comes from cutting meetings, and a smaller share from reduced fatigue. That suggests some of the gain may be available without cutting hours. The two-office audit (+4.1%, uncontrolled) points the same way, but no study has yet compared reorganisation alone with reorganisation plus fewer hours.
- **Headline claims:** The Halden 23.4% figure was inflated, the Varga "entirely an artifact" claim is wrong, and the meta-analysis's "no decay" claim was unsupported.

## Still open

1. Cost per unit of output in discretionary work, including overtime
2. Backlog and statutory-deadline compliance
3. Replication outside a single public employer
4. Effects after evaluation ends
5. A trial arm that reorganises meetings and workflow without cutting hours. That is now the most useful study to run, because it would separate the effect of fewer hours from the effect of removing low-value time.
